title: Ford production system: Model T design, interchangeable-part discipline and 1913 moving assembly specialization
pressure: Growing automobile demand made skilled stationary craft assembly expensive and throughput-limited. Ford's production problem was to make a standardized car cheaply and repeatedly at much larger volume, which required interchangeable parts, process-specific machine tools, flow layout, work sequencing and a different allocation of skill/authority across workers and engineering management.
preExistingWorldModel: Model T production initially used stationary assembly in which small skilled teams worked on cars through many tasks. Moving-process precedents existed in meatpacking, mills, breweries and other industries. Ford production engineers progressively tested moving subassemblies before extending flow to chassis assembly.
candidateRoutes: specialize tasks and move parts/subassemblies between stations
move the whole chassis through a sequenced line
preserve worker flexibility even at lower throughput
observationsAndInstruments: Highland Park built Model Ts for more than three years with stationary assembly, providing a real strong baseline rather than an imaginary preindustrial comparator.
In April 1913 Ford began a crude moving line for magnetos: each worker installed a few parts and moved the unit to the next station; productivity gains motivated expansion.
By late 1913 moving assembly was extended to vehicle production; surviving photographs document unfinished Model Ts moving through Highland Park lines.

Library of Congress history reports assembly labor time falling from roughly 12.5 hours to about 93 minutes under the moving system; Henry Ford archival material records continued refinement into 1914.

The flow system depended on exacting part tolerances/interchangeability and specialized process machinery; electrical unit-drive/flexible machine placement helped arrange equipment according to process sequence.
Worker jobs became narrower/repetitive, and high labor turnover accompanied the new methods, making production throughput and worker experience distinct objectives.
decisiveTests: Moving flow had to outperform an actually operating stationary-team baseline on output/time/cost, not merely appear modern.
Parts had to be interchangeable enough that a downstream station could install them without craft fitting/rework stopping the line.
Line balance had to keep each specialized station within the required cycle time; a local bottleneck could stop the whole system.
Reduced local task flexibility had to be evaluated against declared production goals separately from worker autonomy/turnover/safety.
The line's success on a standardized Model T did not prove that extreme specialization was optimal for low-volume/high-variety production.
technicalOrScientificTransition: Production shifted from product-moving among versatile workers toward work decomposition and material flow through specialized stations. This is a frozen anti-case against unqualified generality: lower local flexibility and stronger specialization generated much higher throughput on a narrow repeated objective when interchangeability and volume made the world compatible.
rivalsAndFailures: Stationary craft assembly was not nonfunctional; it was a strong flexible baseline with lower throughput.
The moving line reused ideas from other industries rather than appearing from one inventor insight.
Extreme specialization reduced local worker discretion/skill variety and coincided with very high turnover, so production productivity is not net human welfare.
Flow-line success depended on standardized product/volume; it does not generalize automatically to high-variety/uncertain work.
Ford's earlier automobile companies failed, showing later production success cannot be projected backward as inevitable managerial superiority.
diffusionAndScaling: Moving assembly and mass-production methods spread through automobiles and other manufacturing. Ford output and affordability increased dramatically as the system matured.
standardsAndInstitutions: Ford production engineering/management allocated process authority centrally; workers executed narrower stations. Supplier/tolerance specifications and internal testing bound external components into the flow.
externalitiesAndCorrections: High productivity coexisted with labor turnover, repetitive work and stronger managerial control; Ford's later wage/social programs addressed labor stability through a separate institutional mechanism rather than changing the physical throughput result.
secondOrderEffects: Mass production transformed manufacturing economics, labor organization, supplier standards and consumer markets. It also generated later counter-movements toward flexible/lean production under different product/quality worlds.
sourceNativeSummary: Ford's 1913 line is deliberately retained as an anti-case to any vague rule that general/flexible work is always superior. A real flexible stationary baseline lost on the declared high-volume Model T objective once interchangeability, machine specialization and demand supported flow. But the gain is scoped: throughput can improve while worker experience and adaptability worsen.
unresolvedHistoricalQuestions: How much of the 1913 throughput gain came from moving conveyance itself versus prior interchangeability/process-machine/layout improvements?
What was the causal contribution of task specialization to labor turnover relative to wages, supervision and local labor-market conditions?
